summary: This part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series defines certificate-based key management, an approach where trusted authorities vouch for the encryption keys that belong to people. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: To lock a message for someone, you need their key and need to be sure it really is theirs. This paper describes trusted introducers who vouch for keys. It is historic.

questions: how does privacy enhanced mail manage keys
what is pem certificate based key management
subtitle: A single worldwide certification hierarchy for the keys behind Privacy Enhanced Mail.

tldr.problem: To encrypt or sign mail, people need each other's public keys and a way to be sure those keys really belong to the named person, and the general X.509 framework leaves too many policy and convention questions open.
tldr.mechanism: A single root, the Internet Policy Registration Authority (IPRA), certifies Policy Certification Authorities (PCAs), which certify Certification Authorities (CAs), which certify users. Certificates are checked up the chain to the IPRA and against revocation lists (CRLs).
tldr.outcome: The memo obsoletes RFC 1114 and is marked Historic in the metadata, so this hierarchy is not a current standard.

today: RFC 1422 obsoletes RFC 1114 and is marked Historic in the metadata. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PEM Needs Key Management
sections.content:
This is one part of a series on privacy enhancement for Internet mail. RFC 1421 defines the message processing, RFC 1423 defines algorithms and identifiers, and RFC 1424 adds supporting services. This part defines the key management architecture, based on public-key certificates, that gives originators and recipients the keys they need.

The architecture is compatible with the CCITT 1988 X.509 framework but goes further. It wants clearly stated certification policies that every user can look up, simple and automated validation despite differing policies, conventions that work before X.500 directory servers are everywhere, and room for patented algorithms. RSA is expected to be the primary signature algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to send a secret note to a friend, you need their lock. This paper explains how to make sure the lock you found really belongs to your friend and not to someone pretending.

sections.title: Certificates and How PEM Uses Them
sections.content:
A certificate contains the name of a user (the subject), that user's public component, and the name of an issuer who vouches that the two belong together. It also carries a validity period, and the issuer signs the whole thing. Names are X.500 Distinguished Names (DNs). The fields are version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer name, validity period, subject name and subject public key.

Because certificates are signed, they can be stored in directories or sent over insecure channels. To send an encrypted message, the originator gets and validates each recipient's certificate, then uses the public component to encrypt the data encryption key (DEK), which encrypts the message. The encrypted DEK goes in the Key-Info field of the header.

For integrity and origin authentication, the originator signs a message integrity code (MIC) with the private component, and puts it in MIC-Info. The originator's certificate can be included in the header so recipients can validate it even without directories.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate is like an ID card that says whose key it is, signed by someone you trust. You check the signature before using the key.

sections.title: The Certification Hierarchy
sections.content:
The hierarchy has a single root, the IPRA, operated under the auspices of the Internet Society. Below it are Policy Certification Authorities (PCAs), each publishing its registration policy as an informational RFC. Below the PCAs are Certification Authorities (CAs), which certify users and subordinate entities. User and mailing list certificates are the leaves. Only PCAs may be certified by the IPRA, and every CA's certification path must lead back to a PCA.

There are three kinds of CA. Organizational CAs certify people with an affiliation to an organization. Residential CAs certify people with no affiliation, until civil authorities may take that role. PERSONA CAs issue certificates to users who want anonymity, and explicitly do not vouch for the user's identity.

Names must stay unique. The IPRA will not certify two PCAs with the same DN, no PCA may certify two CAs with the same DN, and the IPRA keeps databases of hashed DNs to detect duplicates. As a general rule, a CA signs certificates only for subjects whose DN is subordinate to the CA's own DN. Residential CAs are the one exception for duplicate DNs.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one top introducer. Below it are a few introducers who each have their own rules, below those are more introducers, and at the bottom are the people. Each level vouches for the one below.

sections.title: Revocation and Validation
sections.content:
A CA can revoke a certificate if a private component may be compromised or a user's affiliation changes. Revocations are published in a Certificate Revocation List (CRL). The PEM format adds the date of the next scheduled issue, so that a user can tell if a CRL is out of date, and a CA issues a new CRL on that date even if nothing changed. A revoked certificate stays on the CRL until its validity interval expires. The IPRA's CRL is updated monthly.

Every user agent holds the IPRA's public component as the root of its validation. Validating a certificate means checking its signature using the issuer's public component, repeating up the chain to the IPRA, and checking validity periods and the current CRLs. A PCA certificate must not be cached automatically, because adding it means the user accepts that PCA's policy. A validated path to a CA has length two, and a user certificate may need three or more steps.

Software must at least warn the user about expired certificates, missing or old CRLs, and revoked certificates, though local policy may refuse to proceed. Also, the subject DN must be subordinate to the issuer DN unless the issuer is the IPRA or a PCA, or the certificate is invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting a key, you follow the chain of signatures up to the top introducer, and you check a list of cancelled IDs to make sure none of them were cancelled.

sections.title: Private Keys, Policies and Patents
sections.content:
The memo says the secrecy of the user's private component is central to PEM's security, so it must be protected, for example stored encrypted under a passphrase. Key pairs should be generated with unpredictable randomness; seeding a pseudo-random generator only with the date and time is called a poor technique. No CA needs access to a user's private component. If it is lost, encrypted messages become unreadable.

A CA's private component also needs a high level of security, or the guarantee of its certificates is void. Each PCA's policy statement must cover topics such as its identity, scope, security and privacy, certification policy, CRL management, naming conventions and business issues. The IPRA will not license signature algorithms to PCAs, and each PCA must represent that it holds any licenses it needs.

The Patent Statement lists patents on public-key technology held through Public Key Partners. The Security Considerations section itself says only that the entire document is about security.
sections.plainLanguage: The most important thing is to keep your own secret key secret and make it hard to guess. If someone steals the introducer's secret key, every ID it signed becomes worthless.
